summary: This standards-track RFC describes using stateless IP/ICMP translation in IPv6 data centers. IPv4-only clients on the Internet are translated to IPv6 at the edge of the operator's network, and from there the data center can run IPv6 only, simplifying operations.

eli5.summary: Visitors speaking an old language are met at the door by a translator. Inside the building, everyone just uses the new language.

questions: ipv6 only data center with ipv4 clients
what is a siit-dc border relay
subtitle: Run a data center on IPv6 only and let border relays translate legacy IPv4 visitors, without keeping any per-connection state.

tldr.problem: Internet data center operators face IPv4 address scarcity and the extra complexity of running dual stack, while a large share of Internet users still have only IPv4.
tldr.mechanism: SIIT-DC Border Relays translate packets between IPv4 and IPv6 statelessly, using Explicit Address Mappings for service addresses and a translation prefix for client addresses, so the data center itself is IPv6 only.
tldr.outcome: IPv4 clients reach IPv6-only services, their IPv4 source addresses stay visible to applications, and the operator needs far fewer public IPv4 addresses. The RFC also gives MTU and fragmentation guidance.

today: RFC 7755 is a February 2016 document and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It relies on RFC 7757 for explicit address mappings and points to RFC 7756 for the optional Edge Relay.

sections.title: Why Single-Stack IPv6 in the Data Center
sections.content:
Dual stack has historically been the recommended way to move from IPv4 to IPv6. For Internet Data Center (IDC) operators it means running two protocols, which adds complexity and operational overhead, and it does nothing about the depletion of IPv4 addresses. SIIT-DC is an alternative: operate only IPv6 inside, and provide IPv4 connectivity as a service of the network.

The stated design goals are to promote native IPv6 services, keep IPv4 service available to legacy users with no loss of performance or functionality, keep the legacy users' IPv4 addresses visible to nodes and applications in the IPv6 network, conserve public IPv4 addresses, avoid extra complexity on nodes and applications, and be easy to scale and deploy fault-tolerantly.

Because SIIT-DC is stateless, it behaves like a regular IP router: the limiting factors are packets per second and bandwidth, not the number of flows. It allows per-packet load balancing between multiple relays with Equal-Cost Multipath routing, tolerates asymmetric routing, and recovers from a relay failure through normal routing.
sections.eli5: Running two languages inside the building is a lot of work. It is easier to speak one language inside and have a translator at the door.

sections.title: Key Building Blocks
sections.content:
A SIIT-DC Border Relay (BR) is a device or logical function that does stateless IPv4/IPv6 translation, and MUST do so according to RFC 6145 and RFC 7757. An optional Edge Relay (ER), covered in RFC 7756, sits close to IPv4-only components and gives them native-looking IPv4.

Each public-facing service gets an IPv4 Service Address from an IPv4 Service Address Pool (prefixes routed to the BR's IPv4 interface) and an IPv6 Service Address on the actual node. They are paired with an Explicit Address Mapping (EAM) configured in the BR. All other addresses are translated by adding or removing the translation prefix, into which the whole IPv4 address space is mapped using the algorithm of RFC 6052.
sections.eli5: Every shop in the building has an old-language street number and a new-language one, and the translator keeps a list of which matches which. Visitors who are not on the list get a special visitor badge.

sections.title: The SIIT-DC Architecture
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, the pool 192.0.2.0/24 is routed to the BR's IPv4-facing interface. EAM #1 pairs 192.0.2.1 with the IPv6 Service Address 2001:db8:12:34::1, and the translation prefix is 2001:db8:46::/96. Addresses that match no EAM are translated by inserting or removing that prefix. Any number of BRs may exist, as long as they all use the same translation prefix and an identical EAM table.

The IPv6 Service Address should be registered in DNS with an AAAA record and the IPv4 Service Address with an A record. IPv6-capable clients then reach the service natively end to end, while IPv4-only clients come through SIIT-DC. SIIT-DC does not intercept native IPv6 traffic at all, and it needs no change to the underlying IPv6 network.
sections.eli5: Modern visitors walk straight in. Old-language visitors are sent to the translator, and a phone book tells each of them which address to ask for.

sections.title: Packet Flow
sections.content:
An IPv4-only user looks up the A record, then sends a TCP SYN to the IPv4 Service Address. The BR translates it: the destination 192.0.2.1 becomes 2001:db8:12:34::1 through the EAM, and the source 203.0.113.50 becomes 2001:db8:46::203.0.113.50 by adding the translation prefix. The server answers as if the packet had been native IPv6, and the BR translates the reply back.

Neither the client nor the server needs special support. The application may optionally be taught to extract the embedded IPv4 source address from addresses inside the translation prefix, for geolocation, logging or abuse handling.
sections.eli5: The translator rewrites the address on the envelope on the way in and rewrites it again on the way out. The people on both sides never notice.

sections.title: Deployment Guidelines
sections.content:
SIIT-DC suits classic client/server traffic where IPv4 clients start the connection to an IPv6-only service, and HTTP is the RFC's example. Protocols that embed IP addresses in their payload, such as FTP, are problematic and can be handled by adding an ER. Applications that work through standard NAT44 will most likely work through SIIT-DC. Letting IPv6-only applications start connections to IPv4 nodes is possible with DNS64, but all outgoing traffic must then use a source address found in an EAM, or the BR will probably discard it.

For the translation prefix, either a Network-Specific Prefix or the Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96 can be used, but the RFC recommends a Network-Specific Prefix of length /96. Only one Well-Known Prefix exists, and it cannot be used in inter-domain routing. With several BRs, an IGP should advertise the routes so traffic reaches the closest BR. BRs should sit between the IPv4 Internet and the application delivery stack, ideally as a logical function in the routers that already carry the native IPv6 traffic.

To migrate a dual-stack service, designate its native IPv6 address as the IPv6 Service Address, give it an IPv4 Service Address, move traffic by changing the A record, and then reclaim the old IPv4 address. IPv4-translatable IPv6 Service Addresses are possible but discouraged, because they require the whole IPv6 infrastructure to handle translated traffic as a special case.
sections.eli5: The translator works best when visitors come to the building and not the other way round. Put the translator near the front door, and switch services over one at a time.

sections.title: MTU, Fragmentation and ICMP Errors
sections.content:
The IPv6 header is up to 20 bytes larger than the IPv4 header, so a full-size 1500-byte IPv4 packet would become about 1520 bytes in IPv6. For TCP this is handled because the IPv6 node advertises an MSS of 1440 bytes. For other protocols, full-size IPv4 packets with the Don't Fragment flag cleared would need fragmenting by the BR, which can be avoided by raising the Path MTU between the BR and the IPv6 nodes to 1520 bytes or more, without raising the nodes' own MTU.

By default a BR adds a Fragment header when translating an IPv4 packet with DF set to 0, producing an IPv6 Atomic Fragment. The RFC recommends disabling that. The minimum IPv6 link MTU is 1280 bytes while the minimum IPv4 link MTU is 68 bytes, and an IPv4 link with an MTU below 1260 bytes can make an IPv6 node start sending Atomic Fragments. The "second approach" in Section 6 of RFC 6145 avoids this by never reporting an MTU below 1280 and clearing DF for IPv6 packets of 1280 bytes or less.

ICMPv6 errors from routers inside the data center are by default likely discarded by the BR unless their source is IPv4-translatable or covered by an EAM, so operators SHOULD implement RFC 6791 in the BRs.
sections.eli5: The new-language envelope is a bit bigger than the old one. Make sure the roads inside can carry the slightly larger envelope so nothing needs to be cut in half.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The one security issue raised is mistaking the translation prefix for a trusted network. If a Network-Specific Prefix from the provider's own address space is used, services with application-level ACLs that distinguish the operator's networks from the Internet could treat translated IPv4 users as internal. Care MUST be taken to treat the translation prefix like the Internet at large. The operator may also choose a translation prefix that is distinct from, and not a subset of, the prefixes used elsewhere in the infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Visitors wearing the translator's badge could look like they live in the building. Staff must remember that badge means outsider.
